# Reparameterization Estimators

Also called: Reparameterization Trick, Change of Variables Estimators

## Overview
Reparameterization estimators compute [gradients of rendering](#7152-gradient-estimation-and-smoothing.md) integrals by transforming random variables to be independent of scene parameters $\theta$, allowing differentiation to pass through the sampling process via the chain rule [S1]. Unlike standard [automatic differentiation](#7151-automatic-differentiation-reverse-adjoint-mode.md) which fails when sampling distributions depend on parameters (e.g., visibility boundaries moving with geometry), this family rewrites the integral domain to be static [S1, S3]. It sets itself apart from [Adjoint Method](43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) by avoiding the storage of intermediate states for backpropagation, and from [Analytical Gradients](7613-analytical-gradients.md) by handling stochastic sampling rather than deterministic integration [S1].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism relies on the change of variables formula. Let the rendering integral be $I(\theta) = \int f(x, \theta) dx$. If the sampling distribution $p(x|\theta)$ depends on $\theta$, standard differentiation yields biased results due to moving boundaries or support [S1]. The reparameterization trick introduces a parameter-independent random variable $u \sim p(u)$ and a deterministic, differentiable mapping $x = g(u, \theta)$ such that $x$ follows the desired distribution [S1]. The integral becomes:
$$
I(\theta) = \int f(g(u, \theta), \theta) p(u) du
$$
The gradient is then estimated by differentiating the integrand with respect to $\theta$:
$$
\nabla_\theta I(\theta) = \int \nabla_\theta \left[ f(g(u, \theta), \theta) \right] p(u) du
$$
This requires $g$ to be differentiable with respect to $\theta$ [S1]. In volume rendering, this often involves inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the density field to sample ray distances $t$ from uniform noise $u$ [S1]. In path tracing, it involves warping directions or positions to keep visibility discontinuities static in the sample space [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md)
Computes color by sampling ray distances using the inverse CDF of the density field, allowing gradients to back-propagate through sampling locations. Unlike [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)'s hierarchical sampling which uses auxiliary coarse models, this learns sampling points end-to-end. It exhibits lower variance than standard [importance sampling](#9521-importance-sampling.md) with uniform distribution.

### [Boundary Path Integral Formulation](3389-boundary-path-integral-formulation.md)
Estimates derivatives of the path integral with respect to shape parameters by separating differentiation into interior and boundary terms. Unlike siblings that rely on differentiable sampling within the volume, this method converts interior volume integrals into boundary area integrals using the divergence theorem, eliminating the need to evaluate deformation mapping inside the volume.

### [Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering](4798-reparameterized-monte-carlo-volume-rendering.md)
Estimates expected radiance by sampling from the density-induced probability distribution using the reparameterization trick. It sets itself apart from standard Monte Carlo volume rendering by transforming the sampling distribution to depend on parameters via inverse opacity, ensuring the gradient path remains differentiable through the sampling process. It alleviates computational costs by requiring only a few radiance field evaluations per ray.

### [Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE](6332-differential-path-integral-estimator-with-mis-and-nee.md)
Computes the gradient of the rendered image by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space, combining standard BRDF sampling with emitter sampling via NEE. Unlike standard NEE which only connects paths to emitters at the final vertex, this method uses MIS to combine BRDF and emitter sampling probabilities into a single mixture weight, significantly reducing variance for microfacet and mixture BRDFs. It builds on [Reparameterization Estimators](6499-reparameterization-estimators.md).

### [Reparametrized Integral Gradients](6785-reparametrized-integral-gradients.md)
Eliminates bias in gradients caused by visibility discontinuities moving with scene parameters. Unlike explicit edge sampling methods, this method applies a change of variables to transform the integration domain such that discontinuities become static (parameter-independent). It sets itself apart from siblings like [Reparameterized Volume Sampling](3309-reparameterized-volume-sampling.md) by focusing on spherical and path-space reparameterizations to handle visibility changes, rather than volume density variations.

### [Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing](8826-plateau-reduced-differentiable-path-tracing.md)
Alleviates optimization plateaus (regions of zero gradient) by convolving the rendering equation with a smoothing kernel over the parameter space. Unlike standard differentiable renderers that suffer from discontinuous gradients due to visibility changes, [PR-DPT](#8826-plateau-reduced-differentiable-path-tracing.md) ensures that small parameter changes continuously influence the objective function in expectation. It sets itself apart from its siblings by requiring only a forward path tracer and skipping the computation of the renderer's internal gradient tape or adjoint scattering.

### [Monte Carlo Estimation of Differentiable Path Integrals](10814-monte-carlo-estimation-of-differentiable-path-integrals.md)
Estimates the gradient of the differentiable path integral by decomposing the derivative into interior contributions and boundary contributions (derivative of the visibility boundary). It sets itself apart from naive approaches by explicitly handling the discontinuities in visibility (silhouettes and shadow edges) which cause biased gradients if ignored, and by addressing the statistical bias introduced by applying loss functions directly to noisy rendering estimates.

### [Reparameterization](11557-reparameterization.md)
Counteracts parameter-dependent silhouette motion and the resulting bias in differentiated rendering. It solves the problem where changes in scene parameters cause discontinuities in the rendering integral that standard automatic differentiation cannot handle correctly. Unlike its siblings, which may focus on specific sampling strategies or boundary formulations, this method explicitly freezes discontinuities within spherical integrals by tracing auxiliary rays to construct a warp field.

#### PGRIS Estimator
**Definition:** A gradient estimator that uses positivization to handle both positive and negative integrands, achieving theoretical zero-variance convergence of resampled derivative estimates [S1].
**Comparison:** PGRIS uses the integrand as is (with positivization), whereas GRIS without positivization uses the absolute value of the integrand as the target function, leading to higher variance [S1].

#### Bidirectional Estimator for Implicit Surfaces
**Definition:** A Monte Carlo estimator for differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces that performs better than [unidirectional estimators](#3538-unidirectional-volume-boundary-estimator.md) in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials [S2].
**Pitfall:** Unidirectional estimators struggle with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, leading to noisier gradients and less accurate reconstructions [S2].
**Comparison:** Performs better than unidirectional estimators in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, producing cleaner derivative images and smoother optimized shapes [S2].

#### Combined Estimator
**Formula:** The combined estimator is derived by plugging the Monte Carlo-based estimator (Equation 5) into the volume rendering estimator (Equation 3). Equation 5 is: $\hat {L}_\mathrm {o}(\xposof {t}, \dirout ) = \frac {1}{\mcount } \sum _{j=1}^{\mcount } f\lft (\xposof {t}, \superj {\dirin }, \dirout \rgt ) L_\mathrm {i}\lft (\xposof {t}, \superj {\dirin }\rgt ) \lft (\mathbf {n} \cdot \superj {\dirin } \rgt ) \lft / p\lft (\superj {\dirin }\rgt ) \rgt .$ [S3]
**Parameter:** mcount: The number of samples used in the Monte Carlo summation for the estimator [S3].
**Pitfall:** Equation 6 requires recursive evaluation of both the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md) and the rendering equation, which can lead to a rapid increase in computational cost if not handled carefully [S3].

## Background
The reparameterization trick originated in probabilistic graphical models and variational inference [G]. In computer graphics, it was adapted for differentiable rendering to handle the non-differentiable nature of visibility and sampling distributions [S1]. Key developments include the use of [inverse CDF sampling for volume rendering](#1099-inverse-opacity-calculation.md) [S1], boundary path integrals for shape optimization [S2], and warp fields for handling specular discontinuities [S1]. It is widely used in inverse rendering, [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRFs), and differentiable path tracing [S1, S3].
